scope: First reasoned review of the supplied bytes. No specimen was executed. atomscan scores and collector filenames were treated as leads.

samples.identification: Minimal macOS application Info.plist, naming an executable Chrome and icon.icns; no verified publisher or enclosing application supplied.
evidence: All 301 bytes parse as a two-key property-list dictionary. CFBundleExecutable is a declarative relative executable name, not a shell command or code payload. There are no LaunchAgent, interpreter arguments, network settings, scripts, payload bytes or encoded executable data.

The old suspicious matcher did not require CFBundleIdentifier to exist; its claimed mismatch is unsupported here. The old hostile composite only added missing ID/type/version fields. Neither rule established deception, compromised code or any unauthorized action.

Apple documents CFBundleExecutable as the executable filename and lists ID/type/version among recommended Cocoa-app keys. Sparse hand-built packaging and browser wrappers are plausible. The executable name and missing fields merit metadata observations, not an attack verdict.
samples.limits: The named executable and enclosing app are unavailable; this verdict applies to the supplied plist, not an unexamined Chrome executable. Origin and deployment intent remain unknown.

samples.identification: Damaged StormAttack native x86 resource-DLL installer/injector, configured for Active Setup.
evidence: Entry 0x402674 calls WinMain 0x401cb0. Configuration DWORD at RVA 0x4120 equals 3, selecting calls to 0x401900 (Active Setup) and 0x401390 (self-delete).

0x401900 obtains its module filename and creates HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\<generated GUID>. At 0x401a4b it writes the copied executable path to StubPath as REG_EXPAND_SZ. It reads its own image with CRT I/O, patches the copied image, writes it, and launches the copy.

0x401150 constructs a calc/notepad/iexplore target, creates the process, allocates remote memory, writes the DLL path, resolves kernel32!LoadLibraryA and supplies that same function pointer as CreateRemoteThread entry with the remote buffer as argument at 0x40123d.

Alternative mode 1 extracts DLL/101, then 0x401260 deletes/replaces LanmanServer Parameters\ServiceDLL with %SystemRoot%\System32\StormServer.dll before injection. Alternative mode 2 installs/starts an automatic service via 0x401fd0. These are surviving code paths, not proof every path runs in mode 3.

0x401390 obtains the current image short path and COMSPEC, constructs /c del <image> > nul and creates/resumes the cleanup process. Unauthorized durable activation, service-DLL hijacking, foreign-process loading and cleanup together outweigh a benign installer explanation.

The DLL/101 resource at file offset 0x5060 is 39936 bytes, SHA256 0df2765cead245e3a89f9fafbbe5eb42ec7d41386a6c6dc235827539171335fd. It retains Storm ddos DNS / Welcome to use storm ddos / STORM:%d|%s|%s|%s|%s identity/configuration text. Its sections lack execute permissions, imports are absent, raw range 0x1600..0x7400 and entrypoint RVA 0x741a (raw 0x681a) are zeroed. No working DDoS or downloader execution is inferred from those remaining strings.
samples.limits: Stale bound IAT values and hard-coded self-patch offsets limit execution reliability; successful installation is not asserted. No Remcos or WannaCry behavior established. No deployment context was supplied.
samples.trait_decision: Retain every existing finding, including four hostile traits and the suspicious DLL handoff. Embedded PE findings also unchanged.

samples.identification: StormAttack native x86 Active Setup loader with erased resource section.
evidence: The full .text (0x1000..0x3000) and .data (0x4000..0x5000) ranges are byte-identical to the first Windows sample. Independently inspected with Rizin: identical entrypoint, mode 3, self-copy/StubPath write, self-delete, remote LoadLibraryA handoff, and alternative LanmanServer replacement/service-installation code.

The entire declared .rsrc raw range 0x5000..0xf000 is zero-filled. There is no DLL to recover from that section. This prevents claiming successful resource extraction but does not remove the confirmed hostile loader code.
The unsupported collector labels do not control attribution or verdict; surviving code and the StormAttack banner pair identify the loader.
samples.limits: No runtime success, functional DDoS payload, Remcos/WannaCry behavior or deployment context established.
samples.trait_decision: Retain all four hostile traits and the suspicious DLL handoff, all accurately worded as code/API evidence.

trait_changes.claim_correction: Absent identifiers are not mismatched identities. Name plus absent/non-Google-prefix ID does not establish deception. Preserve the exact regex, unless, confidence and plist/Mach-O/macOS scope; remove unsupported T1036.005 mapping.

The conjunction proves a sparse Chrome-named manifest, not malicious impersonation. Preserve all required observations, confidence and plist scope, and the existing test-directory exclusion inherited from the missing-fields property; remove unsupported attack mapping.

consumer_and_fixture_audit: No external exact-ID YAML consumers or old ancestor selectors found; the sole inter-rule consumer is relocated together. The existing check.py consumer was updated. Other macOS masquerade rules are unchanged.

New-ancestor audit: metadata/binary selector in Windows timing-sandbox-evasion downgrade has PE/DLL scope, disjoint from the relocated plist/Mach-O rules. The local Python rule named metadata is a definition, not a root-directory consumer. No metadata/binary/bundle selectors were found.

Existing positive/near-miss controls in testdata/taxonomy/manifest-command-wording/check.py were run before editing (10 pass). Their supposed Chrome attack positive was generated from the same two harmless declarations; it establishes matching, not hostile behavior. Historical review.json cites four earlier macOS malware bundles but explicitly records them as unavailable; no hidden payload or attack behavior could be checked from those bundles.

After editing, 12 controls pass: sparse Chrome, renamed sparse manifest, extra fields, official identity, custom identity, official child identity, plus the existing six wording/execution fixtures. Both relocated findings must be notable. The existing credential-gated remote package execution fixture outside this batch retains its two hostile findings.
All three original specimens were rescanned in slow mode with --no-update and --follow=none. Exact path/hash/member correspondence was checked; no fetched dependencies or PURLs apply.
losses_and_disagreements: Zero observations lost after the two explicit ID mappings; neither Windows file nor the embedded DLL loses any finding or severity. No material attack coverage loss was demonstrated.

The plist loses only unsupported hostile/suspicious interpretations while preserving all 11 findings. Its aggregate probability changes 0.92080176 -> 0.000040690105 (HOSTILE -> BENIGN). The Windows aggregate results remain HOSTILE at 0.9997748 and 0.99. No remaining aggregate classifier disagreement.

The damaged embedded DLL remains ML-benign (0.000849862874019891) with identity/data-reference findings. Its erased code does not justify adding a working payload attack detection to change that score.

Both Windows files get engine-emitted metadata/encoded-payload/url because the printf GUID format {%08X-%04X-...} is mechanically percent-decoded. This is a decoder artifact, not URL encoding intent or network behavior. No YAML rule emits that ID, so a YAML suppressor or duplicate would be inappropriate.

Installed model v18.18 warns that its feature schema is older than extractor v19; this warning is unrelated to YAML validation. Triage pages supplied by the user were inaccessible; no sandbox success was assumed.
